617.title: Har Rai and Har Krishan
617.hook: remember Guru Har Rai, and Guru Har Krishan, seeing whom all pain goes
617.howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember Guru Har Rai and Guru Har Krishan, seeing whom all pain goes; pilgrims visit Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi and take water from its sarovar for the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday: miri piri, and your line: arjan, hargobind. Where did you need calm, and where courage? Today the Ardas names the seventh Guru, and the eighth, who was a child. Day six hundred seventeen.

In the middle of New Delhi, a short walk from the government buildings, there's a white gurdwara with a golden dome and a large pool of water. Every day, people come and carry the water home in bottles: for a sick parent, for a child with a fever, for themselves. Ask why, and you'll hear about a boy. Tradition says a deadly epidemic, remembered as smallpox, was moving through Delhi, and a Guru who was still a child stayed in the city and went among the sick. That place is Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, and the boy is remembered every time the Ardas is said. Today: Har Rai and Har Krishan.
screen: `A WHITE GURDWARA IN NEW DELHI.` → `WATER CARRIED HOME IN BOTTLES.` → `A GURU WHO WAS A CHILD.`

segments.voice: The Ardas line runs on: sri harirai, remember the revered Har Rai. Then: sri harkrishan dhiaaeeai, jis ditthai sabh dukh jaai. Meditate on Har Krishan, seeing whom all pain goes. Guru Har Rai, the seventh Guru, was the grandson of Guru Hargobind. He is remembered for his gentleness. Tradition says he kept a garden and a dispensary of herbal medicines at Kiratpur, open to anyone who needed them, and a well-known story says that once, when his robe brushed a flower and broke it, he was saddened, and spoke about how easily we damage what we can't mend. His son, Har Krishan, became Guru while still a small child. He was called to Delhi, and while he was there, the epidemic broke out. Tradition says he tended the sick in the city, and that he caught the disease himself and died there, still a child. Gurdwara Bangla Sahib stands where he stayed. Now look at what the Ardas says about him. It doesn't call him small, or young, or tragic. It says: seeing him, all pain goes. Dukh, the Punjabi word for pain and sorrow, simply leaves. People who have sat with a sick relative sometimes describe what happens when a small child walks into the room: the air changes. The Ardas takes that ordinary experience and sets it at the heart of the prayer: a child's calm face, and the pain going out of a room. A gentle father, then his child, a Guru who stayed when it was dangerous. Two quiet names in the line.
screen: `HAR RAI: THE GENTLE GURU.` · `A GARDEN, AND A BROKEN FLOWER.` · `HAR KRISHAN STAYED IN DELHI.` · `SEEING HIM, ALL PAIN GOES.` · then, large: `ALL PAIN GOES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture a child's calm face. Sit comfortably, close your eyes if you like, and breathe. Bring to mind a child you know, or once knew, or once were, at a quiet, peaceful moment: asleep, or absorbed in a game. Let their face stay in front of you. Notice what happens in your chest. Let some of today's tension go out on the breath, the way it goes out of a room when a child walks in. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, or the Ardas's own words, sabh dukh jaai, all pain goes. The bell holds the time.
Dukh, pain or sorrow. Seeing Guru Har Krishan, the child Guru who stayed among the sick, all dukh goes.
Your line: all pain goes. Today, be the calm face for someone who's hurting: just sit with them a while. Day six hundred seventeen.

618.title: The nine treasures
618.hook: remember Guru Tegh Bahadur and the nine treasures come running home
618.howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs say that remembering Guru Tegh Bahadur brings the nine treasures running home, and Gurbani often names the Name of God as the true nine treasures.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dukh, and your line: all pain goes. Did you sit with someone who was hurting? Today the Ardas reaches the ninth Guru, the one we spent a month with. Day six hundred eighteen.

There's a strange thing in this line of the Ardas, and once you see it, it's hard to unsee. For the past month we read Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks: the world is a dream, nothing stays, strength gone, all companions gone. And we know how his life ended: arrested, imprisoned, executed in Delhi. By any ordinary measure, he lost everything the world can take. And yet, when the Ardas reaches his name, it promises the opposite of loss. Remember him, it says, and every kind of treasure comes running to your house. How does the man who lost everything become the one who brings everything home? Today: the nine treasures.
screen: `A MONTH OF NOTHING STAYS.` → `HE LOST EVERYTHING THE WORLD TAKES.` → `AND THE ARDAS PROMISES TREASURE.`

segments.voice: The line is: tegh bahaadar simariai, ghar nau nidh aavai dhaai. Remember Tegh Bahadur, and the nine treasures come running home. Nau is nine. Nidh is a treasure, a store of wealth. In old Indian lore, the nine treasures belonged to the god of riches: nine kinds of fabulous wealth, everything a person could want. In ordinary use, nau nidh can stand for every good thing at once. And notice the verb: aavai dhaai, comes running. Not trickles in. Runs, like a child to the door. But Gurbani does something interesting with this phrase. The Sukhmani Sahib, for one, says the nine treasures are the Name of God: whoever has the Name lacks nothing. So the promise in the Ardas works on two levels. On the plain level, Sikhs ask that remembering the ninth Guru bring blessing to their homes. On the deeper level, it echoes his own saloks. What did the last salok say? I have held the Name in my heart; nothing equals it. The man who lost everything the world can take was holding the one treasure it can't. Remember him, and you remember that. Remember, too, his name. He was born Tyag Mal; tradition says he was given the name Tegh Bahadur, brave of the sword, after fighting bravely as a young man beside his father, Guru Hargobind. Brave of the sword, and yet remembered for the treasure he held in his heart. That's the paradox the Ardas sets in one line: the poorest-looking moment, and the richest.
screen: `NAU NIDH: THE NINE TREASURES.` · `AAVAI DHAAI: THEY COME RUNNING.` · `THE REAL TREASURE IS THE NAME.` · `TYAG MAL, BRAVE OF THE SWORD.` · then, large: `NINE TREASURES HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a home full of treasures. Sit and breathe. Picture your home, or a home you love. Then fill it, slowly, but not with money. Put in it the treasures that would actually make it rich: a laugh at the dinner table, someone who listens, a quiet morning, a faith or a hope, a friend who drops by. Name each one as it arrives. Notice which ones are already there. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, as the one treasure Gurbani says holds the rest. The bell holds the time.
Nau nidh, the nine treasures. Every good thing, and in Gurbani, the Name; remember the ninth Guru, and they come running home.
Your line: nine treasures home. Tonight, name one treasure in your home that money didn't buy, out loud, to someone who's part of it. Day six hundred eighteen.

619.title: Help everywhere
619.hook: Guru Gobind Singh, be our help everywhere
619.howItsDone: After remembering the first nine Gurus in Guru Gobind Singh's own stanza, the Ardas names the tenth master, Guru Gobind Singh, and asks him to be the community's help in every place.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nau nidh, and your line: nine treasures home. Which treasure did you name out loud? Today, the tenth Guru, and the last line of the opening stanza. Day six hundred nineteen.

Here's a small detail that's easy to miss when you hear the Ardas at full speed. The opening stanza was written by Guru Gobind Singh. He names Guru Nanak, and then each Guru after him, one by one, all the way to his own father, Guru Tegh Bahadur. And then he stops. He doesn't name himself. Of course he doesn't: it's his poem. But Sikhs who pray the Ardas today hear the tenth Guru's name right after the ninth, with exactly the same words. Someone added it, and the words they chose had been sitting at the end of the stanza all along. Today: help everywhere.
screen: `THE TENTH GURU WROTE THE STANZA.` → `HE STOPS AT HIS FATHER.` → `SOMEONE ADDED HIS NAME.`

segments.voice: Guru Gobind Singh's stanza ends with the words sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai: be our help in every place. Sabh is all. Thaaeen is places. Sahaai, our old friend, is the helper. So the Var's opening ends by asking all the Gurus it has named to be our help, everywhere. Then the Ardas, as Sikhs pray it, continues: dasvaan paatshaah, sri guru gobind singh sahib ji, sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai. The tenth master, Guru Gobind Singh, be our help in every place. The community took the poem's last line and gave it to the poet. The poet, who left himself out, is written back in. And it fits him. Guru Gobind Singh's life covered nearly every kind of place a person can be. He became Guru as a boy after his father's execution. He wrote poetry and, tradition says, kept a court of poets at Anandpur. He founded the Khalsa. He fought battles, lost his sons, and lived through siege, flight and grief. And before his death, Sikh tradition says, he ended the line of human Gurus and told the Sikhs that the Guru from then on would be the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, with the Khalsa community. So be our help everywhere isn't a vague wish. It's asked of someone remembered in the court and on the battlefield, in the forest and in grief. Sikhs ask him to be present in every place they go: the job interview, the hospital waiting room, the long drive home. Notice, too, that the prayer doesn't ask for help in some places. Sabh thaaeen. All of them.
screen: `SABH THAAEEN: IN EVERY PLACE.` · `THE POEM'S LINE, GIVEN TO THE POET.` · `A LIFE THAT WENT EVERYWHERE.` · `ALL PLACES, NOT SOME.` · then, large: `HELP EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for help in one place. Sit and breathe. Think through the places you'll be today or this week: your desk, your car, a hard conversation, a waiting room, your own kitchen late at night. Pick the one where you feel most alone. Picture yourself there. If you pray, you can ask, in the Ardas's own words, sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai, be our help in every place, and feel that it includes this one. If you don't, picture someone you trust standing beside you there. The bell holds the time.
Help everywhere. Sabh thaaeen hoi sahaai: the last line of the tenth Guru's stanza, which the Ardas gives back to him.
Your line: present in every place. When you arrive at the place you pictured, pause at the door for one breath and say the line. Day six hundred nineteen.

620.title: The light of the ten
620.hook: the Ardas turns to the Guru Granth Sahib, the embodied light of the ten Gurus
620.tomorrow: The five, the four, the forty
620.howItsDone: After naming the ten Gurus, the Ardas turns to the Guru Granth Sahib as the light of the ten masters, and the sangat answers Waheguru aloud; Sikhs bow before it and treat it as the living Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday: help everywhere, and your line: present in every place. Did you pause at a door and say it? The Ardas has now named all ten Gurus. Today it turns to the one in front of the room. Day six hundred twenty.

At a candlelight vigil, the first candle is lit with a match. After that, no one uses a match again. Each person tips their wick into the flame of the person next to them, and the light moves down the line. By the end there are hundreds of candles, but in a sense there's only ever been one flame, passed along. Sikhs have used an image very like this for more than four hundred years, to describe how the Guruship moved from Guru Nanak to the next Guru and the next. And the Ardas, having named all ten, now says where that flame is today. Today: the light of the ten.
screen: `ONE MATCH, THEN NO MORE.` → `WICK TO FLAME, DOWN THE LINE.` → `HUNDREDS OF CANDLES, ONE FLAME.`

segments.voice: After the tenth Guru, the Ardas continues: dasaan paatshaaheeaan dee jot, sri guru granth sahib ji. The light of the ten masters, the Guru Granth Sahib. Jot means light, a flame, the kind that burns in a lamp. In paraphrase, the line goes on: fixing your mind on its reading and the sight of it, say Waheguru! And here, for the first time in the Ardas, the whole room answers aloud: Waheguru. The idea of one light passing on is old. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the bards Satta and Balwand sang that when Guru Nanak installed Guru Angad, it was the same light and the same way; only the body was changed. Sikhs understand each Guru as carrying the one jot, the one flame, in a new body, ten times. Then in 1708, tradition says, Guru Gobind Singh passed the Guruship not to a person but to the scripture. So the flame that went from candle to candle now burns in a book. That's why Sikhs treat the Guru Granth Sahib not as a book about the Guru, but as the Guru. It rests on a raised seat under a canopy. Someone waves a chaur, a whisk, over it as it's read. At night it's carried to its own room to rest. People bow when they enter its presence. To someone outside, that can look like honoring an object. Sikhs would say it's honoring a presence: the light of all ten, in one place, still speaking. The ten in one. And the Ardas, every time it's prayed, turns toward it.
screen: `JOT: THE LIGHT IN THE LAMP.` · `SAME LIGHT, ONLY THE BODY CHANGED.` · `THE FLAME NOW BURNS IN A BOOK.` · `HONORING A PRESENCE.` · then, large: `THE TEN IN ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a page of the Granth. If you can, open one, in a gurdwara or on a screen; any Ang will do. If not, picture it: the Gurmukhi letters in long lines, the cloth around it, the canopy above. Let your eyes rest on the page without trying to read it all. Just look, the way you'd look at a candle flame. Think of ten lives passing one light down. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, the room's answer, once, quietly. The bell holds the time.
Jot, light, a flame. Dasaan paatshaaheeaan dee jot: one jot, carried by ten Gurus, now burning in the Guru Granth Sahib.
Your line: the ten in one. If you see a candle or a lamp lit today, let it remind you of the flame passed down the line. Day six hundred twenty.

621.title: The five, the four, the forty
621.hook: it remembers the Panj Pyare, the four Sahibzade and the forty liberated
621.howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember the Panj Pyare, the four Sahibzade and the forty Muktas in one line; five initiated Sikhs still lead every amrit ceremony, and the Sahibzade's martyrdom is marked each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jot, and your line: the ten in one. Did a candle or a lamp remind you of the flame? Now the Ardas turns from the Gurus to the Sikhs who stood with them. Day six hundred twenty-one.

Three numbers. Say them fast and they sound like a phone number: five, four, forty. Each number is a group of people. One group stepped forward when everyone else stepped back. One group was four brothers, two of them still small boys. One group walked away from their Guru, and then came back. The Ardas says all three numbers in a single breath, right after the Guru Granth Sahib, before any other Sikhs it remembers. Today: the five, the four, the forty.
screen: `FIVE, FOUR, FORTY.` → `THREE GROUPS OF PEOPLE.` → `SAID IN ONE BREATH.`

segments.voice: The line goes: panjaan piaariaan, chauhaan sahibzaadiaan, chaaleeaan mukteaan. The five beloved, the four princes, the forty liberated. The five: the Panj Pyare. At Vaisakhi at Anandpur, Sikh tradition says Guru Gobind Singh stood before a huge gathering with a sword and asked for someone willing to give their head. A long silence. Then one man stood. Then four more. As the story is told, they came from different castes and regions: a shopkeeper, a farmer, a water carrier, a washerman, a barber. They were the first initiated into the Khalsa, and Sikhs say the Guru then asked them to initiate him. Ever since, five initiated Sikhs lead the amrit ceremony. The four: the Sahibzade, the Guru's sons. The two older ones, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, died fighting at Chamkaur. The two younger ones, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, still small boys, were captured and executed at Sirhind after, tradition says, refusing to give up their faith. Sikhs mark their martyrdom every year. The forty: the Chali Mukte. During the siege of Anandpur, a group of Sikhs left the Guru and, tradition says, signed a paper disowning him. At home, they were shamed for it, and a woman named Mai Bhago led them back. They fought at Khidrana, now Muktsar, and fell. As the last of them was dying, the story goes, the Guru tore up the paper. That's why they're called mukte, the liberated. Five who stepped forward. Four who held on. Forty who came back. Sikhs hear in them three ways a person can be faithful.
screen: `THE FIVE: WHO STOOD UP.` · `THE FOUR: THE GURU'S SONS.` · `THE FORTY: WHO CAME BACK.` · `THREE WAYS TO BE FAITHFUL.` · then, large: `FIVE, FOUR, FORTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say five, four, forty. Sit and breathe. On one out-breath, say: five, and picture people standing up in a silent crowd. On the next: four, and picture four brothers, two grown and two small. On the next: forty, and picture people walking back toward someone they'd left. Repeat it slowly. Notice which of the three you understand best right now: stepping forward, holding on, or coming back. If you pray, you can follow with Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
The five. The Panj Pyare who stood up, the four Sahibzade, and the forty who came back: remembered in one breath.
Your line: five, four, forty. If there's someone you've drifted from, take one small step back toward them today. Day six hundred twenty-one.

622.title: The steadfast and the sharers
622.hook: the steadfast, those who meditated, shared food, ran the kitchen and wielded the sword
622.howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember the steadfast, those who meditated, shared their food, ran the langar and wielded the sword; vand chhakna, sharing, is counted among the three pillars of Sikh life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five, and your line: five, four, forty. Did you take a small step back toward someone? Today the Ardas widens out from famous groups to people with no names at all. Day six hundred twenty-two.

In a gurdwara kitchen somewhere, a woman has been on her feet since five in the morning. She's rolled more rotis than anyone could count. Nobody knows her full name; the kids just call her auntie ji. She'll never be in a history book. Out front, a man has swept the same gurdwara steps every Sunday for thirty years. The Ardas, having remembered the five, the four and the forty, now remembers people like them: not by name, but by what they did with their hands and their days. It's a list of verbs. Today: the steadfast and the sharers.
screen: `AUNTIE JI, SINCE FIVE A.M.` → `THE MAN WHO SWEEPS THE STEPS.` → `REMEMBERED BY WHAT THEY DID.`

segments.voice: Listen to the run of the line: hathiaan, japiaan, tapiaan. The hathi are the steadfast: people who held firm, who wouldn't be moved off their faith. The japi are those who repeated and recited, who kept the Name and the banis going day after day. The tapi are those who lived with discipline and endured hardship. Then a list of what they did: jinhaan naam japiaa, who meditated on the Name. Vand chhakiaa, who shared what they had and then ate. Deg chalaaee, who kept the cooking pot going, who ran the langar. Tegh vaahee, who wielded the sword, who protected others. Notice that vand chhakiaa is one of the three things Sikhs often call the pillars of the faith: naam japna, remembering the Name; kirat karni, honest work; and vand chhakna, sharing. Sikh teachers like to point to the word order: vand comes first, then chhak. Share, then eat. Not eat and share the leftovers. Notice, too, how the kitchen and the sword sit side by side. Deg and tegh: feeding and protecting are named together, as two halves of looking after people. We'll come back to those two words later in the Ardas. And then the line names what these people left behind: their kamaaee. It's a word for earnings, what you earn by labor. The Ardas asks the room to fix its mind on the kamaaee of these beloved, truthful ones. Not their fame. Their earnings, built up quietly, meal by meal and morning by morning. So every time Sikhs pray, they remember people like auntie ji in the kitchen, even if no one there knows her name.
screen: `HATHI, JAPI, TAPI: THE STEADFAST.` · `VAND CHHAKIAA: SHARE, THEN EAT.` · `THE POT AND THE SWORD, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `KAMAAEE: WHAT THEY EARNED.` · then, large: `THE SHARERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan to share one meal. Sit and breathe. Think through today's meals. Pick one you could share: cook a little extra for a neighbor, take a coworker to lunch, set an extra place, give something to a food bank. Or simply serve someone else first at your own table. Picture yourself doing it, share first, then eat. Notice how small the act is, and how old. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you decide. The bell holds the time.
Kamaaee, earnings built up quietly, meal by meal and morning by morning. Hathi, japi, tapi; those who shared, then ate, kept the pot going and held the sword: remembered for their kamaaee.
Your line: the sharers. Share one meal today, or serve someone else first, and don't mention it. Day six hundred twenty-two.

screen: `DAY 622 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THOSE WHO SAW AND OVERLOOKED.`

623.title: Those who saw and overlooked
623.hook: those who saw others' faults and chose to overlook them
623.howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember those who saw others' faults and overlooked them, dekh ke andith keetaa, alongside the steadfast and those who shared, served and protected.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kamaaee, and your line: the sharers. Did you share a meal, or serve someone first? This week ran from dukh through nau nidh, help everywhere, jot, five, four, forty, and the sharers. Today, the last verb in that list. Day six hundred twenty-three.

Your roommate leaves the dishes again. A coworker takes credit for something you did. Your brother says the thing he always says at family dinners. You see it. You absolutely see it. And then there's a fork in the road, a split second where you decide what to do with what you saw. There's usually a well-worn path at that fork: we file it away, we bring it up later, we tell someone else. The Ardas, in its list of people Sikhs remember with honor, includes one group whose only deed is what they did at that fork. Today: those who saw and overlooked.
screen: `THE DISHES, AGAIN.` → `YOU SEE IT.` → `A FORK IN THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Right after those who shared their food, ran the kitchen and wielded the sword, the Ardas adds: dekh ke andith keetaa. Dekh ke: having seen. Andith: unseen. Keetaa: made it. Having seen, they made it unseen. It's a striking phrase. It doesn't say they didn't notice. They weren't naive. They saw clearly, and then they chose to treat it as if they hadn't. Sikhs hear it first about other people's faults and the wrongs done to them: they saw, and they let it go. Some also hear it about temptation: they saw what could have pulled them off course, and looked away. Gurbani has the same spirit elsewhere. Among the saloks of Sheikh Farid, the Sufi saint whose verses are in the Guru Granth Sahib, one says, in paraphrase: do good even to the one who does you harm, and don't let anger settle in your mind. Now, an important balance. The very same line of the Ardas honors those who wielded the sword. So overlooking isn't pretending injustice doesn't exist, or refusing to protect people. A Sikh is asked to stand up against cruelty. Andith is about something smaller and more daily: the slights, the irritations, the faults of the people around you that you could keep score of, and don't. A family, a friendship, a shared kitchen: each runs partly on people who quietly decided not to mention it. The Ardas puts them on the same list as the steadfast and those who wielded the sword. Their deed was invisible on purpose. That's the point.
screen: `DEKH KE: HAVING SEEN.` · `ANDITH KEETAA: THEY MADE IT UNSEEN.` · `FARID: DO GOOD TO THE ONE WHO HARMS.` · `NOT INJUSTICE: THE DAILY SLIGHTS.` · then, large: `SEE, AND OVERLOOK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one fault to overlook today. Sit and breathe. Let one small irritation come to mind, something someone does that you keep noticing. Not a real wrong that needs facing; something small. See it clearly, once. Then picture yourself setting it down, the way you'd put a pebble from your shoe back on the path. Notice the urge to pick it up again. Let it pass. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you set it down. The bell holds the time.
Andith, unseen. Dekh ke andith keetaa: having seen clearly, they chose to make it unseen.
Your line: see, and overlook. When the small fault you chose shows up today, see it, and let it go without a word. Day six hundred twenty-three.
